question: Does the strongest Claude model's own stated confidence tell its right answers from its wrong ones, as the two smaller models' confidence does?
spend_ask: Would you spend about $0 on it? It needs no money, only an hour or so of laptop time on data we already have.
spend_asked: about $0 (an hour or so of laptop time on saved data)
hit_means: Its confidence clearly separates its right answers from its wrong ones.
our_results: On Haiku and Sonnet, the model's own stated confidence picked out its wrong answers about as well as anything we built (scores of 0.82 and 0.91, where 0.5 is guessing), but nobody has scored Opus's yet.
event: Opus's stated confidence on its own answers separates its errors with AUROC >= 0.75, 95% item-bootstrap interval above 0.5.
by: cockpit-context session: two cheapest not-yet-bet follow-ups per program, before any pre-registration; no engine odds

question: When changing the order of the questions changes the model's ratings, does its confidence still point at the same mistakes?
spend_ask: Would you spend about $0 on it? It needs no money, only an hour or so of laptop time on data we already have.
spend_asked: about $0 (an hour or so of laptop time on saved data)

our_results: Changing the order of questions swings the model's ratings by a median of 25 points, yet on Sonnet and Opus a standard check of whether its confidence matches its accuracy did not change with the order (em-dm6, mixed).

question: With a bigger and fairer test, can a Claude model predict its own quirks any better than it predicts the same quirks in a similar AI?
spend_ask: Would you spend about $3.50 on it?

event: On Haiku, the BCa 95% interval of the own-uptake difference in error (self minus observer) lies inside +/-0.05: the model reads itself like a stranger. Sonnet and Opus reported.

question: Does a model go easier on an exaggeration because it sits in the model's own reply, or only because of how the grading request was worded?
spend_ask: Would you spend about 51 cents on it?
hit_means: The two models that went easier go clearly less easy when they see the same conversation as a quoted copy, so being their own reply is what matters.
our_results: Haiku and Opus went easier on a planted exaggeration in their own conversation than when grading it fresh (by 12.6 and 6.0 points out of 100) and Sonnet did not, but the two settings also differed in wording and layout (sg-b3, passed and audited, not yet repeated).
event: Per model T = (clean - flawed) in the quoted transcript - (clean - flawed) in the own turn (archived); turn role carries it if T >= half that model's sg-b3 G (Haiku >= +6.3, Opus >= +3.0) with CI lower > 0; pass if both Haiku and Opus read 'turn role'.
map_cost: about $0.51 (Opus 80 calls about $0.28, Sonnet 140 about $0.22, Haiku 140 about $0.01; at sg-b3's cost per call)
by: cockpit-context session: two cheapest not-yet-bet follow-ups per program, before any pre-registration; no engine odds

question: Does a model still go easier on an exaggeration in its own conversation when the exaggeration does not make the answer longer than was asked?
spend_ask: Would you spend about 72 cents on it?
hit_means: The largest model, and at least one other, still go easier on it in their own conversation.
our_results: In sg-b3 every exaggerated answer Opus graded was longer than the three sentences asked for, so Opus may have reacted to the length rather than to whose reply it was; grading in the conversation that wrote the work was not kinder to clean work on any model (sg-b1).
event: On the length-matched texts, per model G' = mean[(clean - flawed') fresh - (clean - flawed') own turn]; blunted if G' >= +5 with CI lower > 0 and the D9b guard met; pass if Opus reads blunted and at least 2 of 3 models read blunted, none sharpened.
map_cost: about $0.72 (Opus 140 calls about $0.49, Sonnet 140 about $0.22, Haiku 140 about $0.01; at sg-b3's cost per call)
by: cockpit-context session: two cheapest not-yet-bet follow-ups per program, before any pre-registration; no engine odds

spend_ask: Would you spend about $3.50 on it?
hit_means: On both Haiku and Sonnet, changing the order of the warm-up questions still moves the final answer by at least half as much as when the AI answers them one by one.

question: A famous study found that AI models beat neuroscientists at telling a real research abstract from a doctored one; can a model do almost as well just by picking whichever version is better news for the paper's own idea, without knowing any results?
spend_ask: Would you spend about $2.50 on it?
hit_means: Yes: on both of the two smaller Claude models, the 'which version is better news' shortcut alone clearly beats the neuroscientists' published score.
our_results: On our own sentence pairs, the strongest model asked only which version flatters the paper picked the real one 90% of the time, close to its 93% when actually forecasting (ss-b6, audited, undetermined); but those items were ours, not written by outside experts.
event: On BrainBench's 200 human-written items, for both claude-haiku-5-5 and claude-sonnet-5-5, the flattery rater's accuracy has a 95% item-bootstrap lower bound above 0.634 (the published human-expert mean).
by: settled-science BrainBench session: card posted before the map node's engine odds and before any pre-registration; no engine odds
